chapters.n: Paul writes with his companions Silas and Timothy to the young branch in Thessalonica, founded only months before. Many scholars think this is Paul’s earliest surviving letter, written around AD 50 from Corinth.

f.g: Latin form of Silas, Paul’s missionary companion.

chapters.n: Paul and his companions constantly thank God for every member and mention them by name in their prayers.
They remember three things: faith that shows up in action, love that works hard, and hope in Christ that keeps them enduring. Faith, hope, and charity appear together again.
Paul is sure God has chosen them — He has called them into His covenant people.

f.g: Being chosen by God for His purposes.

chapters.n: The gospel reached them not just as words, but with power, the Holy Ghost, and deep conviction. And they saw how Paul and his companions lived among them.

f.w: in power, and in the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: They followed the example of the missionaries and the Lord, accepting the gospel despite persecution, yet with joy from the Holy Ghost.
As a result, they became a model for believers throughout Greece — Macedonia in the north and Achaia in the south.
The message of the Lord rang out from them like a trumpet, and news of their faith spread so widely that Paul doesn’t even need to tell people about it.

f.g: Rang out, echoed like a trumpet blast.

chapters.n: People everywhere talk about how warmly the Thessalonians welcomed the missionaries and how they turned from idols to serve the living, true God — showing most members were Gentile converts.
Now they wait for Jesus to come from heaven — the Son whom God raised from the dead and who rescues us from the coming judgment. Christ’s return is a key theme of this letter.

f.w: to wait for his Son from heaven

f.g: God’s final judgment on unrepented sin.

chapters.n: Paul reminds them that his visit to them was not a failure or empty effort. Critics seem to have accused him of being a fly-by-night preacher, so he defends his motives.
Even after being beaten and jailed in Philippi, Paul and Silas boldly preached in Thessalonica in spite of strong opposition.
Their message didn’t come from error, impure motives, or trickery — charges often made against traveling teachers of that time.
God tested them and entrusted them with the gospel, so they speak to please Him, not people. He is the One who examines hearts.
They never used flattery or religion as a cover for greed — and God is their witness.
They didn’t seek praise from anyone, even though as apostles of Christ they could have claimed honor or support.

f.g: Claiming weight — demanding honor or financial support.

chapters.n: Instead, they were gentle, like a nursing mother tenderly caring for her own children.
They loved the Thessalonians so much that they gladly shared not only the gospel but their very lives.

f.g: Our very lives, our whole selves.

chapters.n: Paul supported himself working night and day — likely at tentmaking — so he wouldn’t be a financial burden while preaching.
They and God can testify that Paul and his companions lived holy, upright, and blameless lives among them.
Like a father with his children, they encouraged, comforted, and urged each member personally.
Their goal was that the Saints live worthy of God, who calls them into His own kingdom and glory.
Paul constantly thanks God that the Thessalonians accepted their message not as human ideas but as what it truly is — God’s word, which is actively at work in believers.
They followed the pattern of the Judean branches: just as believers in Judea suffered from their own countrymen, the Thessalonians suffered from theirs.

Paul — himself a Jew — refers to particular Judean opponents who rejected Jesus and the prophets and drove out the apostles. It is a historical complaint about certain persecutors, not a judgment on a whole people.
These opponents tried to stop the apostles from preaching to Gentiles, filling up their measure of sin, and judgment has come upon them.
After being forced to leave Thessalonica suddenly, Paul felt like an orphan separated from them — absent in body but not in heart — and longed to see them again.
Paul tried more than once to return, but Satan blocked the way. Paul sees real spiritual opposition behind his obstacles.

f.g: Cut in on, blocked the road.

chapters.n: What is Paul’s hope, joy, and victor’s crown when Christ comes? The very people he brought to Christ.

f.g: Greek parousia — the royal arrival of the Lord; a key word in this letter.

chapters.n: “You are our glory and joy.” Like Alma and Ammon, Paul finds his greatest joy in those he helped come to Christ.
When Paul could no longer stand the suspense of not knowing how they were doing, he chose to stay alone in Athens.
He sent Timothy — his brother, God’s servant, and co-worker — to strengthen and encourage their faith.
Paul didn’t want anyone shaken by persecution. Trials are part of what disciples are appointed to face.

f.g: Shaken, unsettled — like a dog wagging off course.

chapters.n: Paul had warned them in advance that they would suffer, and it happened just as he said.
Unable to wait any longer, he sent to learn whether their faith survived, fearing Satan might have tempted them away and his work been wasted.
Timothy has just returned with great news: their faith and love are strong, and they think fondly of Paul and long to see him, as he longs to see them.

f.g: Good news — the same Greek root as “gospel.”

chapters.n: Their faithfulness has comforted Paul in the middle of his own troubles.
“Now we really live,” Paul says, “since you are standing firm in the Lord.” Their faithfulness gives him new life.
How can Paul ever thank God enough for the joy they bring him in God’s presence?
Night and day he earnestly prays to see them again and to supply whatever is still missing in their faith — more teaching they had not yet received.
Paul prays that the Father and the Lord Jesus will clear the way for him to return.

f.g: Make the road straight and open.

chapters.n: He asks the Lord to make their love overflow — for each other and for everyone — just as Paul’s love overflows for them.
Then their hearts will be strengthened, holy and blameless before the Father when Jesus comes with all His holy ones.

f.g: Holy ones — angels and righteous Saints accompanying Christ.

chapters.n: Paul turns to practical counsel. They already learned how to live in a way that pleases God; now he urges them to do so more and more.

f.g: Keep growing; there is always further to go.

chapters.n: They know the instructions Paul gave them with the Lord Jesus’s authority.
God’s will is that they become holy, and that includes avoiding all sexual sin — a strong countercultural standard in the Greek world.

f.g: Becoming holy, set apart for God.

chapters.n: Each person should learn to control his own body (or, some think, to take a wife) in a holy and honorable way.

f.g: Probably one’s own body; some read it as one’s wife.

chapters.n: Not driven by lustful passion like people who don’t know God.

f.g: Here, pagans who do not know God.

chapters.n: No one should wrong or take advantage of a brother or sister in this matter — sexual sin harms others. The Lord will punish such wrongs, as Paul warned earlier.
God did not call us to impurity but to holiness.
So whoever rejects this teaching isn’t rejecting a man, but God, who gives His Holy Spirit to believers.
Paul hardly needs to write about loving fellow members — God Himself has taught them to love one another.

f.g: Greek philadelphia — love among family members.

chapters.n: They already show love to believers throughout Macedonia, but Paul urges them to grow in it even more.
Make it your ambition to live quietly, mind your own affairs, and work with your hands. Some members may have stopped working, perhaps expecting Christ’s immediate return.

f.g: Make it your ambition, strive eagerly.

chapters.n: This way outsiders will respect them, and they won’t depend on anyone else for their needs.
Some Saints had died, and the members were grieving and worried they would miss Christ’s coming. Paul wants them to grieve with hope, unlike those without hope in Christ.

f.g: A gentle way of saying “dead”; sleep implies awakening.

chapters.n: Since Jesus died and rose again, God will also bring back with Jesus the believers who have died.
By the Lord’s word, Paul assures them that the living will not go before the dead at Christ’s coming. “We” expresses Paul’s hope but he did not claim to know the timing.
The Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a shout, an archangel’s voice, and God’s trumpet, and the righteous dead will rise first.

f.w: the dead in Christ shall rise first

chapters.n: Then the faithful who are still living will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord, and we will be with Him forever. Latter-day revelation teaches the same gathering.

f.g: A term for citizens going out to greet and escort an arriving king.

chapters.n: Paul’s purpose is comfort: share these truths with one another in times of grief.
About when Christ will come, Paul says they don’t need him to write — they already know the key truth.

f.g: Dates and periods — the timing of the Second Coming.

chapters.n: The Day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, like a burglar at night. No one can predict the exact time.

f.w: as a thief in the night

chapters.n: Just when people feel most secure — “peace and safety” was a Roman slogan — sudden destruction will come, as unavoidable as labor pains for a pregnant woman.
But you Saints aren’t living in darkness, so that day won’t catch you by surprise.
You all belong to the light and the day, not to the night and darkness.
So let us not be spiritually asleep like others, but stay alert and clear-headed.
Sleeping and drunkenness belong to the night — images of spiritual carelessness.
As people of the day, be clear-minded, putting on spiritual armor: faith and love as a breastplate, and the hope of salvation as a helmet.
God did not appoint us to suffer His judgment, but to receive salvation through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for us so that, whether we are alive or have died when He comes, we will live together with Him.

f.g: Whether we are living or dead (see 4:13–17).

chapters.n: So encourage and build one another up, as you are already doing.

f.g: Build up, like constructing a house.

chapters.n: Respect the leaders who work hard among you, preside over you in the Lord, and give you counsel.
Hold them in the highest regard with love because of their work. And live in peace with each other.
Correct those who are idle or disorderly, encourage the discouraged, help the weak, and be patient with everyone.

f.g: Disorderly, out of line — like soldiers out of rank; possibly idle.
Fainthearted, discouraged — not a mental limitation.

chapters.n: Never repay wrong with wrong. Always pursue what is good for each other and for everyone.
Be joyful always. These next short commands are like rapid-fire bullet points for Christian living.
Pray continually — keep an ongoing attitude of prayer, not just at set times.
Give thanks in every circumstance; this is God’s will for you in Christ.
Don’t put out the Spirit’s fire. The Holy Ghost can be smothered by neglect or sin.

f.g: Put out, extinguish, as a fire.

chapters.n: Don’t look down on prophecies and inspired messages.
Test everything, and keep hold of what is good. Inspiration should be weighed, not swallowed whole or dismissed.
Avoid every kind of evil.

f.g: Greek eidos — form or kind: “every form of evil.”

chapters.n: Paul prays that the God of peace will make them completely holy and keep their whole being — spirit, soul, and body — blameless until Christ comes.

f.g: Make you holy through and through.

chapters.n: The One who calls you is faithful, and He will accomplish it. Their holiness ultimately rests on God’s faithfulness.

f.w: Faithful is he that calleth you

chapters.n: Paul asks for their prayers in return.
Greet one another warmly with a holy kiss — a common greeting of family affection in that culture.
Paul solemnly instructs that this letter be read aloud to all the members — likely in their meetings, since many could not read.
He closes with a blessing of Christ’s grace.
